title: Bahrain GP 2026: Practice Sessions Analysis & Race Predictions
summary: Kimi Antonelli's 1:36.302 in FP3 was the only front-running lap with nothing left on the table: his weekend-best sectors all came on one lap. Max Verstappen sits just 0.155s back on aggregated pace with 0.123s still unused, while Liam Lawson hides the biggest untapped potential in the field at a massive 0.677s.

sections.heading: The Headline: Antonelli Builds the Perfect Lap
sections.content:
Kimi Antonelli didn't just top the final practice session in Bahrain. He produced the one lap of the weekend that left nothing on the table. His 1:36.302 in FP3 was the fastest single lap across all three sessions, and when we stitch together every driver's best sectors from the entire weekend, it still sits on top. His weekend-best Sector 1 (24.979), Sector 2 (31.661) and Sector 3 (39.662) all came on the same lap. No other driver in the top five managed that except Isack Hadjar.

Max Verstappen is the man closest to him, and the aggregated data says he is closer than the timesheet suggests. Officially, Verstappen's best was 1:36.580, 0.278s adrift. But his combined best sectors add up to 1:36.457, just 0.155s behind Antonelli. The difference comes almost entirely from Sector 1: Verstappen's 24.911, the quickest opening sector of anyone all weekend, came on an earlier lap in FP3, not on his flying lap. That is 0.123s he has already proven he can find.

Behind them, George Russell's aggregated 1:36.716 puts the second Mercedes third, 0.414s off his teammate. Then comes the closest fight of the weekend: Charles Leclerc (1:36.858) and Hadjar (1:36.860) are separated by just 0.002s on ultimate pace. Lando Norris completes the top six at 1:37.000, with Lewis Hamilton (1:37.041) and Oscar Piastri (1:37.188) just behind.

The official sessions told a three-way story: Verstappen topped FP1 with 1:37.520, Leclerc took FP2 with 1:37.528 and Antonelli owned FP3. Our aggregated analysis, which you won't find on any official timing source, sharpens that picture. Mercedes and Red Bull are the two cars at the front, Ferrari is a step behind, and McLaren is losing out heavily in one specific part of the lap despite Norris setting the fastest final sector of the weekend.

sections.heading: Sector-by-Sector Breakdown
sections.content:
Sector 1 belongs to Red Bull. Verstappen's 24.911 is the benchmark, with Antonelli (24.979) and Hadjar (25.002) the only other drivers to get under or level with the 25-second mark. Both Red Bulls sit in the top three here, which points to strong traction and straight-line efficiency out of the opening corners. Further down the order, Pierre Gasly's 25.132 and Carlos Sainz's 25.146 were quicker than Russell's best opening sector, a sign that the Alpine and Williams are competitive in a straight line even if the rest of the lap holds them back.

Sector 2 is where Mercedes wins the weekend. Antonelli's 31.661 is 0.192s faster than Verstappen's 31.853, and Russell (31.925) is the only other driver under 31.95. Leclerc (31.963) and Hamilton (32.034) keep Ferrari in touch, but McLaren is badly exposed: Piastri's best is 32.166 and Norris's 32.225, more than half a second behind Antonelli. Sector 2 alone accounts for 0.564s of the 0.698s gap between Norris and the top.

Sector 3 tells a different story. Norris's 39.567 is the fastest final sector of the weekend, ahead of Antonelli (39.662), Verstappen (39.693), Russell (39.717), Hadjar (39.745) and Piastri (39.767). The McLaren clearly comes alive in the closing section, which makes its Sector 2 deficit even more striking: this is a car that can win individual parts of the lap but can't currently string a competitive lap together.

Put the top two side by side and the picture is clear. Verstappen gains 0.068s on Antonelli in Sector 1, but loses 0.192s in Sector 2 and another 0.031s in Sector 3. Net: 0.155s to Mercedes. If Red Bull can claw back even a tenth in the middle sector, pole becomes a coin toss.

sections.heading: Understanding Aggregated vs Actual Times
sections.content:
Official timing shows only one number per driver: their fastest complete lap. That hides a lot. A driver can set the quickest Sector 1 of their session on one lap, the quickest Sector 2 on another and the quickest Sector 3 on a third, but none of it shows up unless it all happens on the same lap. Our aggregated time takes each driver's best Sector 1, best Sector 2 and best Sector 3 across all three practice sessions and adds them together. The result is a theoretical optimal lap: what the car and driver have already proven they can do, piece by piece.

The gap between that aggregated lap and the driver's best actual lap is the key number. A delta close to zero means the driver is putting everything together when it matters. Antonelli, Hadjar and Hamilton all recorded a delta of exactly 0.000 this weekend. A large delta means there is speed in the car that hasn't yet been assembled into one lap, and that is usually where qualifying surprises come from.

That's why we use aggregated times for qualifying predictions. In Q3, with fresh softs, low fuel and maximum commitment, drivers tend to nail the sectors they have already shown they can. This analysis is unique to RaceTrace and isn't available on F1.com or any official timing source. This weekend it flags one driver in particular: Liam Lawson, whose 0.677s delta is the largest of any front-half runner.

sections.heading: Practice Session Evolution: FP1 to FP3
sections.content:
FP1 was a Red Bull statement. Verstappen's 1:37.520 put him 0.383s clear of Russell, with Hadjar third at 1:38.303. McLaren had a session to forget: Piastri (1:39.276) and Norris (1:39.293) finished 11th and 12th, more than 1.7s off the pace. Mercedes looked solid but unspectacular, with Antonelli fifth at 1:38.580.

FP2 reshuffled the order. Leclerc topped the session with 1:37.528, ahead of Hadjar (1:37.627) and Norris (1:37.665), with McLaren recovering more than 1.6s from FP1. The aggregated data is revealing here: Leclerc's FP2 aggregated lap was 1:37.453, meaning even his session-topping effort left 0.075s behind. Russell's FP2 delta was even bigger: 1:37.714 aggregated against 1:38.020 actual, a 0.306s gap that hid the Mercedes' true pace and dropped him to seventh on the official timesheet.

FP3 brought the biggest jump. Antonelli's 1:36.302 was 2.278s faster than his FP1 best, by far the largest improvement among the front-runners, while Verstappen improved by 0.940s. Mercedes found the most in Sector 2 as the track rubbered in and the car was dialled in. Franco Colapinto delivered the most dramatic turnaround: after a troubled FP2 with only two sets used and a best of 1:43.391, he finished FP3 ninth with 1:37.920, ahead of teammate Gasly on actual pace.

sections.heading: Tyre Strategy Analysis
sections.content:
This was a soft-heavy weekend for almost everyone. Among the front-runners, Piastri was the most aggressive, using eight sets of softs across practice, five of them in FP2 alone. Russell used seven, and Antonelli, Leclerc, Hadjar and Norris six each. At the other end, Verstappen and Hamilton used just five sets of softs each, which leaves them with more fresh rubber for qualifying than most of their rivals.

The most significant tyre story is the hard compound, or rather the lack of it. Leclerc was the only driver in the entire field to run the hard tyre, completing two sets in FP3. Every other team arrives at the race with no direct practice data on the hardest compound. If the race turns into a medium-hard affair, Ferrari will be the only team that has actually seen how the hard behaves on this surface.

Mercedes leaned on the medium more than anyone at the front: Antonelli used five sets of mediums, the most among the top teams, while Red Bull, McLaren and Ferrari stayed closer to two to four. That's a useful sign for Sunday, as Mercedes should have the best understanding of the compound most teams are likely to start on.

Race implications: expect most of the grid to start on mediums with a plan to switch to hards. Those with limited hard-tyre knowledge will be judging the second stint on the fly, which creates real risk of strategy errors and makes the timing of the first stop critical.

sections.heading: Key Findings and Surprises
sections.content:
1. Mercedes owns the middle of the lap. Antonelli's 31.661 in Sector 2 is 0.192s clear of anyone in another car, and it is the main reason he sits on top of the aggregated order. With both Mercedes in the top three on ultimate pace, the Silver Arrows are the team to beat over one lap.

2. Lawson is the hidden story of the weekend. On official timing he finished the weekend 15th, with a best of 1:38.266. On aggregated pace he is ninth, at 1:37.589. That 0.677s delta is the largest of any front-half driver, and his FP3 Sector 1 (25.141) was quicker than Russell's best. If he puts it together in qualifying, a Q3 appearance is very much on.

3. The midfield is razor-thin. Gasly (1:37.918) and Colapinto (1:37.920) are 0.002s apart on aggregated pace, with Arvid Lindblad (1:38.064), Gabriel Bortoleto (1:38.077) and Fernando Alonso (1:38.173) all within a quarter of a second. Gasly's 0.323s delta suggests Alpine have more in hand than the official timesheet shows.

4. McLaren's problem is specific, not general. Norris has the fastest Sector 3 of the weekend, yet he is 0.698s off on aggregated pace because of a 0.564s deficit in Sector 2. Whatever is costing them there, it is costing them the front row.

5. Ferrari's hard-tyre gamble. Leclerc was the only driver to run the hard compound all weekend. It may have cost him short-run preparation time, but it could pay off handsomely if the race hinges on the hard tyre.

sections.heading: Race Day Predictions
sections.content:
Qualifying Prediction: Based on aggregated pace, we expect Antonelli to take pole with a time around 1:36.0, as track evolution and fresh softs push the field beyond the FP3 benchmark. Verstappen should line up alongside him: if he finds the 0.123s already sitting in his Sector 1, the gap to pole could shrink below a tenth. Russell completes our predicted top three. Watch for Lawson, whose 0.677s of untapped pace could carry him well beyond his official practice position.

Race Prediction: We're backing Verstappen to win. Antonelli has the edge over one lap, but Verstappen was quick in every session (first in FP1, fourth in FP2, second in FP3) and has saved more fresh softs than his rivals. Over a race distance, Red Bull's consistency and his racecraft should beat Mercedes' Sector 2 advantage. Expect a medium-hard one-stop for most front-runners, with the first stop window decided by how the hard tyre behaves, something only Ferrari has seen in practice.

Podium Prediction: 1. Max Verstappen (Red Bull Racing), 2. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes), 3. George Russell (Mercedes).

Wildcard Factors: The lack of hard-tyre data across the field is the biggest unknown. A team that misjudges degradation on the second stint could lose several positions, and an early safety car could tempt teams into an unplanned switch to hards. Ferrari, with the only real data on that compound, are best placed to take advantage.

Dark Horse and Key Battle: Lawson is our dark horse for a strong points finish if he converts his hidden pace in qualifying. The key battle to watch is Leclerc versus Hadjar: separated by just 0.002s on aggregated pace, they are likely to start close and fight over fourth for the entire race.
